title: Five Myths about the Current Memory Boom - Semiwiki
gist: SemiWiki argues the current AI-driven memory boom is a pricing and capacity-allocation story rather than a pure HBM or new-fab shortage: DDR5 and NAND are surging alongside HBM, bit volume growth is normal, market shares are stable, and durable manufacturing barriers protect incumbents like Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix from new entrants.

insights.claim: The current semiconductor memory boom is primarily an AI-driven capacity-allocation problem rather than simply a shortage of fabs or factories.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Investors should track allocation and pricing dynamics, not just fab construction/capex announcements, when assessing when memory supply normalizes.

insights.claim: During the current AI memory boom, industry-wide memory revenue has risen roughly 5x and profits roughly 10x.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Signals extraordinary margin expansion across memory suppliers; watch upcoming earnings for whether this pace is sustained or peaking.
insights.quote: Memory revenue has gone up 5x. Profits 10x.

insights.claim: HBM currently carries roughly the same profit margin as ordinary DDR5 memory, undercutting the narrative that HBM alone explains the industry's profit surge.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Investors overweighting pure-play HBM exposure may be missing that DDR5 and NAND pricing are equally important profit drivers.
insights.quote: HBM is currently the same margin as DDR5.
insights.locator: Is it just HBM causing this?

insights.claim: AI servers contain more than 5x as many DDR5 bits as HBM bits, meaning ordinary DRAM volume dwarfs HBM volume even in AI-focused systems.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: DDR5 pricing trends matter as much as HBM allocation news for forecasting memory supplier revenue from AI buildouts.
insights.quote: There are >5x more DDR5 Bits in an AI server than BHBM bits.
insights.locator: Is it just HBM causing this?

insights.claim: HBM accounts for only about 20% of total DRAM bits shipped, so most DRAM revenue upside is coming from broader DDR5 demand and pricing, not HBM alone.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Reframes DRAM investment theses around aggregate DDR5 pricing power rather than HBM market share alone.
insights.locator: Is it just HBM causing this?

insights.claim: NAND flash prices have skyrocketed in tandem with DRAM prices during the AI boom, and NAND supplier SanDisk has seen its stock price and profits surge as a result.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: The AI memory boom is broader than DRAM/HBM; NAND-focused suppliers like SanDisk are also direct beneficiaries worth tracking.
insights.quote: NAND prices have skyrocketed like DRAM. Sandisk stock prices and profits skyrocketed as well.
insights.locator: Is it just HBM causing this?

themes.theme: Price, not volume, drives the revenue surge

insights.claim: Memory bit shipment growth during the current boom is running at roughly 20% year-over-year, about the same rate as the prior five years, indicating volume growth itself is not unusual.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Rules out a simple 'much more memory being shipped' explanation; the boom must be understood through pricing, not unit growth.
insights.quote: Memory bits are growing by about the same as past 5 years. 20% YoY.
insights.locator: Memory bit growth is causing revenue to skyrocket

insights.claim: The surge in memory revenue and profit is driven almost entirely by customers paying 3-5x more per bit for the same technology, not by any increase in bit shipment volumes.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Because this is a pure pricing story rather than a structural supply-demand volume shift, it could unwind faster than a capacity-driven boom if buyer willingness to pay softens.
insights.quote: Same bits, same technology, more money.
insights.locator: Memory bit growth is causing revenue to skyrocket

themes.theme: Market share is stable, not reshuffling

insights.claim: Despite temporary disruptions (SK Hynix's early HBM ramp lead, Samsung's failure to deliver, Micron's delayed HBM entry), overall memory market shares today are within 2% of where they stood 10 years ago.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Undercuts narratives of a major competitive reordering among incumbent memory makers; positioning among SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron has proven durable.
insights.quote: Overall market shares today are within 2% of 10 years ago.
insights.locator: The memory leaders are shifting and the order is changing

insights.claim: Chinese memory makers YMTC (NAND) and CXMT (DRAM) are the genuinely new entrants gaining share and are expected to grow to roughly 8% of the market over the next few years, supply the author says the market needs.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Watch YMTC and CXMT capacity ramps as the main source of incremental global memory supply and a potential check on pricing over the next few years.
insights.quote: YMTC in NAND and CXMT in DRAM are the new players and they will grow to about 8% of market over the next few years.
insights.locator: The memory leaders are shifting and the order is changing

themes.theme: This cycle vs. past memory cycles

insights.claim: Unlike prior memory cycles, in this boom customers are signing long-term supply agreements and both datacenter buyers and memory suppliers are profiting simultaneously, rather than following the historical pattern of a price boom followed by below-cost selling.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Long-term contracts could dampen the severity of the next downturn versus historical memory busts, a structural change worth monitoring in supplier guidance.
insights.quote: Customers have shown willingness to spend 5x more per bit, sign long term agreements, and both the datacenter customers and the memory suppliers are making tons of money.
insights.locator: This is the same old memory cycle

insights.claim: The industry's last severe memory downturn, when prices fell below cost, occurred in 2023, consistent with a roughly four-year historical cycle length.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Provides a historical cadence reference point for timing when the current up-cycle might eventually turn.
insights.locator: This is the same old memory cycle

insights.claim: A price correction in memory is still expected eventually, but the author believes it will likely be milder than the 2023 crash given strong demand from multiple sources, while acknowledging uncertainty about how prices could keep rising this fast.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Sets an expectation for investors: a correction is coming, but current strong multi-source AI demand argues against a repeat of the severe 2023 crash.
insights.quote: It will correct, but not that bad (hopefully).
insights.locator: This is the same old memory cycle

themes.theme: Barriers protect incumbents from new entrants

insights.claim: High memory margins would normally attract new competitors, but memory fabs require different tooling than logic fabs, and the design, product, and manufacturing expertise needed takes years to develop at every level from executives to junior engineers.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Explains why elevated memory margins are unlikely to be quickly competed away by new fab entrants, supporting a longer runway for incumbent pricing power.
insights.locator: Other companies will start making memory, spoiling the party

insights.claim: Even TSMC, described as the best fab company in the world, would likely be unable to match Micron's memory bit cost within eight years if it started making memory today, illustrating the durability of manufacturing know-how as a barrier to entry.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Incumbent memory makers (Micron, Samsung, SK Hynix, SanDisk) have a durable cost moat that new entrants, even top-tier foundries, cannot quickly close, supporting sustained pricing power.
insights.quote: If TSMC (best Fab company in the world) started today, I am not sure they could match Micron on bit cost in 8 years.
insights.locator: Other companies will start making memory, spoiling the party
